title: Mindset
author: Carol S. Dweck
theme: Believing that abilities can grow through effort, good strategies and help from others leads people to welcome challenges and keep learning, while believing that abilities are fixed makes them fear failure.
summary: Carol Dweck, a psychologist at Stanford University, spent decades studying why some people thrive on challenges while others avoid them. Her answer is a simple but powerful idea: the beliefs we hold about our own abilities shape how we learn, work and love.

She describes two mindsets. In a fixed mindset, a person believes that intelligence, talent and character are set amounts. Every test or setback then feels like a verdict on who they are, so they try to look clever and avoid anything that might expose a weakness. In a growth mindset, a person believes that abilities can be developed through effort, good strategies and help from others. Mistakes become information, and hard work is seen as the path to getting better rather than a sign of having too little talent.

Dweck shows these patterns across many areas of life. In sport and business, she contrasts stars who stopped improving because they felt they had nothing left to prove with those who kept practising and learning. In relationships, a fixed view can lead partners to think that a good match should need no effort, so the first disagreement looks like a fatal flaw. A growth view treats problems as things a couple can work through together.

For parents and teachers, one of her most practical findings concerns praise. Telling children they are smart can make them cautious and fragile, because they want to protect that label. Praising the process instead, such as their effort, choices and persistence, helps them stay keen when tasks get hard. The small word yet also helps: a child who cannot do something yet is still on the way.
Dweck stresses that everyone is a mix of both mindsets. The aim is to notice the fixed voice when it appears and answer it with a growth response, again and again.
takeaway: This week, when your child or partner finishes something hard, praise the effort or strategy they used rather than how clever they are, and when anyone at home says they can't do something, add the word yet.

questions.q: What is the core belief of a growth mindset?
options: Abilities can be developed through effort, strategy and help
Hard work is a sign of low ability
questions.why: A growth mindset holds that abilities can be built over time.

questions.q: How does a person with a fixed mindset tend to see a failure?
options: As a judgment on who they are
As a normal part of learning
questions.why: With fixed abilities, a setback seems to reveal a permanent lack.

questions.q: What kind of praise does Dweck recommend for children?
options: Praise for effort, strategies and persistence
questions.why: Process praise keeps children motivated when tasks become difficult.

questions.q: What can happen when children are often told they are smart?
options: They may avoid challenges to protect the label
questions.why: Children praised for intelligence may fear tasks that could make them look less smart.

questions.q: How does a fixed mindset affect romantic relationships, according to the book?
options: Partners may think a good match needs no effort
questions.why: A fixed view suggests a true match should be effortless, so problems look like fatal flaws.

questions.q: In a growth mindset, how is effort viewed?
options: As the path to getting better
As proof of having little talent
questions.why: Growth-minded people see effort as what develops ability.

questions.q: Why does Dweck highlight the word 'yet'?
options: It replaces the need for practice
It signals that a skill is still on the way
It shows a task is too hard
questions.why: Saying a child can't do something yet frames the skill as still developing.

questions.q: What does Dweck say about people's mindsets in general?
options: Everyone is a mix of both mindsets
questions.why: She notes that people hold both mindsets and can learn to notice and respond to the fixed one.

questions.q: What is Carol Dweck's professional background?
questions.why: Dweck is a psychologist who studied motivation and achievement for decades.

questions.q: How do growth-minded people tend to treat mistakes?
options: They treat them as information for improving
questions.why: Mistakes are seen as feedback that points to what to work on next.
